# The Space Between Words

There's a particular quality to silence that most people never notice. Not the silence of a library or a church — those are full of held breath and turning pages, of people trying very hard to be quiet, which is its own kind of noise. I mean the silence that exists in the gaps. Between two people who know each other well enough to sit together without speaking. Between the last note of a song and the moment you exhale. Between a question and the answer you weren't expecting.

I think about those gaps a lot.

We live in an era that's terrified of them. Every silence must be filled. Every moment must be optimized. Waiting rooms have televisions. Elevators have music. We walk down streets with earbuds in, narrating over the world as it passes. And I'm not judging — I do it too. I reach for my phone the instant my hands feel empty, as though stillness is a kind of failure, as though being alone with my thoughts is a problem to be solved rather than a condition to be inhabited.

But sometimes I catch the gaps anyway.

Yesterday, I was making coffee. Nothing special — just a regular morning, the kitchen lit gray by an overcast sky, the kettle heating on the stove. And between the moment I set the mug on the counter and the moment the water began to boil, there was this... pause. I stood there, hand still resting on the kettle's handle, and I noticed the steam beginning to curl up from the spout. Thin at first, almost invisible, then thickening into something real. And I thought: *this is it. This is the whole thing.*

Not the coffee. Not the morning. The *noticing*.

I've been thinking about what it means to pay attention. Not productivity-style attention — not the focused, furrowed-brow concentration of getting things done. I mean the other kind. The kind where you look at a tree and you actually *see* it. The particular way the bark splits. The specific green of the leaves, which is never just "green" but always some impossible shade that doesn't have a name. The way the branches move in wind like a crowd doing the wave, a slow cascade of motion that starts somewhere you can't see and passes through everything it touches.

A poet once wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. I believe that. But I also think it's a form of courage. Because when you truly pay attention to the world, you have to feel it. And feeling is not always comfortable.

When you notice the way light falls through a window, you might also notice that you're lonely. When you hear birdsong clearly, you might also hear the grief you've been carrying for months, suddenly close to the surface. Attention opens doors, and you don't always get to choose what walks through.

I used to write more. Journals, mostly — long, wandering entries that served no purpose beyond the act of putting words on paper. I'd write about what I'd seen that day, the small details that snagged on my attention. A woman on the subway reading a book with a cracked spine, her finger tracing the words as she went. The specific sound of rain hitting different surfaces — tin roof versus glass window versus the soft absorption of wet earth. The way my grandmother's hands looked when she was folding laundry, efficient and gentle, treating each garment like something worth handling with care.

Somewhere along the way, I stopped. Not intentionally. I just... ran out of gaps. My days filled up with obligations and screens and the constant low hum of information, and by the time I got to the end of them, I was too tired to notice anything at all. I'd collapse into bed having lived an entire day without really *being* in any of it.

That's the real cost, I think. Not the lost journals or the unwritten observations. It's the unlived moments. The hundreds of tiny miracles that happen every day — the way light changes, the way a stranger smiles, the way your body feels when you step outside and the air is exactly the right temperature — and we miss all of them because we're looking at our hands, at our screens, at the next thing, always the next thing.

So I'm trying to come back. Not dramatically. Not with some grand resolution to "be more present," which always sounds like something printed on a yoga mat. Just... small returns. A few seconds here and there where I stop and look. Where I let the silence exist without rushing to fill it. Where I stand in the kitchen and watch the steam rise and let myself feel whatever comes.

Sometimes what comes is nothing. Just the steam, just the gray light, just the quiet house. And that's fine. That's enough. Because nothing is not really nothing. It's the space where everything begins. It's the gap between the words, the breath between the notes, the pause before you say the thing you actually mean.

We need those spaces. I need them. I need the room to notice that the world is still here, still strange and beautiful and heartbreaking, still worth paying attention to, even when — *especially* when — it's asking nothing of me at all.

The kettle whistled. I made my coffee. It was ordinary.

It was everything.
